Impermissible means not allowed. When something is impermissible, it is forbidden — it crosses a line that must not be crossed, whether that line is drawn by a law, a rule, a moral principle, or an accepted standard.

It is the direct opposite of permissible, which means allowed or acceptable. The prefix "im-" simply flips the meaning to the negative.
What Makes It Different From Just "Not Allowed"

Here is where the word gets interesting. "Impermissible" doesn't just describe something that's discouraged or frowned upon. It describes something that is actively prohibited — something that violates a rule, a standard, or an authority that has the power to forbid it.

Think of it this way: eating pizza for breakfast is unusual, maybe odd to some people, but nobody would call it impermissible. However, a judge declaring someone guilty without giving them a fair trial? That is impermissible — it violates the law and principles of justice.

The word carries a sense of seriousness and finality. When something is labeled impermissible, it's not a suggestion to avoid it. It's a firm declaration that it must not happen.

"Impermissible" is a formal word. You will almost never hear it in casual conversation. Instead, you'll encounter it in:

  • Legal settings — court documents, rulings, laws
  • Academic writing — philosophy, ethics, policy papers
  • Professional guidelines — medical ethics, corporate rules, codes of conduct
  • Formal discussions — government, institutions, organizations

In everyday speech, people say "not allowed," "forbidden," or "off-limits." But in formal writing or official contexts, "impermissible" is the precise, authoritative way to say it.
Who or What Decides That Something Is Impermissible?

This is a crucial part of understanding the word. Something doesn't just become impermissible on its own — there is always a source of authority declaring it so. That authority can be:

  • The law — a government or court that prohibits certain actions
  • An institution — a school, hospital, or company with its own rules
  • A moral or ethical framework — a set of principles that says certain actions are wrong
  • A religious code — doctrines that forbid certain behaviors
  • A professional standard — the rules that govern doctors, lawyers, judges, etc.

For example, if a school says students cannot use their phones during exams, using a phone during an exam is impermissible under that school's rules. If a country's constitution says the government cannot imprison citizens without a trial, doing so is constitutionally impermissible.

Yes. Impermissible is a binary, absolute word. Something is either impermissible or it is not. You cannot say something is "a little impermissible" or "slightly impermissible" — that would be like saying something is "a little forbidden." The word draws a hard, clear line.

Here are examples across different contexts so you can see how naturally the word fits:

  • "Using someone else's work and claiming it as your own is impermissible in academic institutions."
  • "The evidence was collected illegally and is therefore impermissible in court."
  • "Many ethical frameworks argue that deliberately harming an innocent person is morally impermissible."
  • "Discrimination based on race or gender is impermissible under this company's policy."
  • "The treaty makes the use of certain chemical weapons impermissible under international law."

Notice how in every case, there's an underlying authority (academic rules, courts, ethics, company policy, international law) that is doing the forbidding.

These words share a similar idea, though with subtle differences in feel:

  • Forbidden — general and widely understood; slightly more dramatic in tone
  • Prohibited — very close in meaning; often used in legal and official contexts
  • Inadmissible — most commonly used in legal settings (e.g., inadmissible evidence)
  • Unauthorized — means done without official permission or approval
  • Unlawful / Illegal — specifically violates a law (narrower than impermissible)
  • Unacceptable — informal; something that falls below a standard or expectation

Impermissible is the most formal and precise among these, and it works across legal, ethical, and institutional contexts equally well.

• Permissible — allowed, acceptable
  • Authorized — officially approved
  • Lawful / Legal — in accordance with the law
  • Acceptable — meeting the required standard

Impermissible means something is not allowed because it violates a rule, law, moral principle, or standard — and it is said with formal authority and finality.

Once you see this word, ask yourself: What is the authority here, and what line is being crossed? That question will always unlock the full meaning in context.
